title: Relativistic velocity addition
theory: Choose the laboratory as frame S and the moving spacecraft as S′. In one dimension, if S′ moves at v relative to S and the object moves at u′ relative to S′, its laboratory velocity is u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²). The signs encode direction. This relationship replaces simple addition at high speed and reduces to that approximation when the correction term is very small.

A spacecraft moving at 0.600c launches an object forward at 0.500c in the spacecraft frame. Classical addition predicts 1.100c, exposing the failure of the approximation. The relativistic denominator is 1.300 and the laboratory result is 0.846c. If the spacecraft emits forward light instead, substituting u′ = c gives u = c, consistent with the invariant vacuum light speed.

For the inverse transformation use u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²). Name the observer for every reported velocity and keep all quantities in matching units. The equation is for collinear velocities; do not apply it componentwise without the appropriate multidimensional transformation.

model.q: A spacecraft travels at 0.600c and ejects a probe backward at 0.400c in its own frame. Find the probe's laboratory velocity.
steps: With forward positive, v = +0.600c and u′ = −0.400c.
u = 0.200c/0.760 = +0.263c: the probe still travels forward in the laboratory.

guided.q: A spacecraft moves at 0.500c and a forward probe moves at 0.500c relative to it. Predict whether the laboratory speed reaches c, then calculate it.

exam.q: A spacecraft at 0.800c emits light backward. Determine its laboratory velocity using relativistic velocity addition and interpret the result.
points: Use v = +0.800c and u′ = −c.
The light travels backward at vacuum speed c in the laboratory too.

claim: Light emitted backward by a moving spacecraft travels more slowly than c in the laboratory.

title: Young's double slit and single-particle interference
theory: Two coherent slits produce waves with a stable relative phase. At a screen point their path difference determines constructive or destructive interference. For narrow slits and a distant screen, in-phase slits have bright fringes where path difference is nλ. The central maximum corresponds to equal path lengths.

In the small-angle geometry, adjacent bright-fringe spacing is Δy = λL/d, where L is slit-to-screen distance and d is slit separation. Increasing wavelength or screen distance increases the spacing; increasing slit separation decreases it. The formula is a geometric approximation and its symbols must not be swapped.

Individual photons or electrons arrive as localised detections, but many detections accumulate into an interference pattern when coherence is retained. This is evidence for wave–particle duality. Determining which slit each particle uses changes the experimental conditions and generally removes the interference pattern.

model.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through slits separated by 0.300 mm onto a screen 2.00 m away. Find fringe spacing.
steps: Convert λ = 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m and d = 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Use Δy = λL/d in the small-angle model.

guided.q: Keep the wavelength and slit separation unchanged but move that screen to 1.00 m. Find the spacing.
steps: Fringe spacing is directly proportional to L.

exam.q: In the same small-angle setup, the slit separation doubles while wavelength and screen distance stay fixed. Predict the fringe spacing change and explain what single-photon detections show.
points: Δy is inversely proportional to slit separation, so spacing halves.
Each photon gives a localised detection.
Many detections build the interference pattern, demonstrating wave-like statistical behaviour.

claim: A single-photon experiment cannot produce an interference pattern after many detections.

title: Polarisation and the transverse nature of light
theory: An electromagnetic wave has electric and magnetic field oscillations perpendicular to each other and to propagation. Polarisation specifies the electric-field oscillation direction or pattern. A simple linear polariser transmits one field component, demonstrating a transverse wave property. A purely longitudinal sound wave has no equivalent transverse oscillation direction to select.

For ideal linearly polarised light, a second polariser at angle θ to the first transmits intensity I = I₀cos²θ. This quantitative relation is used here as an extension model. Parallel axes maximise transmission; crossed axes give zero in the ideal model. Distinguish the field-amplitude projection from its squared intensity relationship.

Real filters are imperfect and absorb energy. For ideal unpolarised incident light, the first polariser transmits half the intensity before any second-filter calculation. Do not apply that half factor again when the incoming beam is already aligned linearly polarised light.

model.q: Already polarised light of intensity 80.0 W m⁻² passes through an ideal analyser 60.0° from its polarisation axis. Find transmitted intensity.
steps: The light is already polarised, so no initial half-intensity factor is needed.
Use the stated extension model I = I₀cos²θ.

guided.q: The analyser turns to 45.0°. What intensity is transmitted from that 80.0 W m⁻² already polarised beam?
steps: The transmitted intensity is 40.0 W m⁻².

exam.q: Explain why ideal crossed polarisers block linearly polarised light and why this supports a transverse model.
points: The second transmission axis is perpendicular to the first polarisation direction.
The electric field has no component along the second axis in the ideal model.
Selecting an oscillation direction perpendicular to travel is a transverse-wave property.

claim: Ordinary longitudinal sound in air can be polarised with the same transverse-axis mechanism as light.

title: Black-body spectra and the origin of quantum theory
theory: An ideal black body absorbs all incident radiation and emits a temperature-dependent continuous spectrum. As temperature rises, the spectrum's peak shifts to shorter wavelength and its total emitted power increases. A black body need not look black when hot: its visible emission can be bright. The peak wavelength is not the only wavelength emitted.

Classical equipartition predictions failed at short wavelengths, producing the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck introduced discrete oscillator energies to explain the measured spectral shape. Quantum theory emerged to address a specific experimental failure, rather than because wave phenomena disappeared.

As an extension calculation, Wien's displacement relationship λmaxT = b uses absolute temperature and b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K. A wavelength-form spectrum and a frequency-form spectrum have different peak locations, so use the stated representation. Real objects can depart from ideal black-body behaviour through wavelength-dependent emissivity.

model.q: Estimate the peak wavelength of a 5800 K ideal black body using the stated Wien extension model.
steps: The wavelength peak is 500 nm, while the object emits a broad spectrum.

guided.q: If the temperature doubles in this model, what happens to the wavelength peak?
steps: λmax is inversely proportional to T.
The peak shifts to shorter wavelength; it is not the whole spectrum's single wavelength.

exam.q: Describe two changes to a black-body spectrum when temperature rises, and state what the ultraviolet catastrophe challenged.
points: The wavelength peak moves to shorter wavelength.
The total emitted power increases.
The observed short-wavelength spectrum contradicted the classical prediction and motivated quantised-energy modelling.

claim: A black body emits radiation at only its peak wavelength.

title: Determining Planck's constant from photoelectric data
theory: The photoelectric energy equation Kmax = hf − φ predicts a linear relationship between maximum electron kinetic energy and incident frequency. A stopping potential measures Kmax through eVs, so Vs = (h/e)f − φ/e. The graph's slope is h/e, not h, when its vertical axis is voltage.

Use a spread of above-threshold frequencies and determine a best-fit slope from widely separated points on the fitted line. The horizontal intercept estimates threshold frequency and the vertical intercept gives −φ/e. An intercept is an extrapolated model quantity; the source does not produce negative photoelectron kinetic energies below threshold.

Control the surface and measurement conditions, convert frequency-axis scale factors correctly and distinguish intensity from frequency. Repeating measurements can reduce random uncertainty, while a voltmeter offset may systematically shift the intercept. A straight-line fit does not justify ignoring anomalous points without investigating their cause.

model.q: A Vs-versus-f best-fit gradient is 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s. Estimate h using e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
steps: The graph equation gives gradient = h/e.
h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, using C V = J.

guided.q: The graph's voltage intercept is −2.00 V. Find the work function in eV and joules using e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

exam.q: On a Kmax-versus-frequency graph with energy in joules, identify the slope and intercept and explain why intensity does not set the slope.
points: The slope is h.
The vertical intercept is −φ.
Intensity changes photon arrival rate; the energy-per-photon relation hf determines the frequency dependence.

claim: The gradient of every photoelectric graph is Planck's constant regardless of the axes.

title: Fluorescence, phosphorescence and energy levels
theory: An absorbed photon can excite an atom or molecule into a higher energy state. Some energy may be transferred non-radiatively before an emitted photon is produced. The emitted photon can therefore have lower energy and longer wavelength than the absorbed photon. Energy is conserved across both radiative and non-radiative transfers.

Fluorescence is prompt emission following excitation and typically ends rapidly when the excitation source is removed. Phosphorescence involves longer-lived states and can persist after the source is removed. Persistence does not mean energy is being created: stored excitation energy is released over time.

Applications include fluorescent markers, forensic visualisation and glow materials. A useful explanation connects the excitation wavelength, allowed energy changes and emission behaviour. The simple level diagram is a model; real molecular spectra contain additional vibrational and environmental structure.

model.q: A material absorbs a 4.00 eV photon, transfers 1.00 eV non-radiatively and emits one photon. Find the emitted energy and wavelength using hc = 1240 eV nm.
steps: Emitted wavelength is 413 nm, longer than the 310 nm absorbed wavelength.

guided.q: If the absorbed energy remains 4.00 eV but 2.00 eV is transferred non-radiatively, find the emitted wavelength.
steps: The emitted photon has energy 2.00 eV.

exam.q: Explain why a glow material can emit after its lamp is switched off without violating conservation of energy, and distinguish phosphorescence from prompt fluorescence.
points: Excitation energy was stored while the material was illuminated.
Phosphorescence releases energy through longer-lived states after illumination ends.
Prompt fluorescence normally ceases rapidly when excitation is removed; neither process creates energy.

claim: A phosphorescent material creates new energy because it glows after the external light is removed.

title: Continuous and characteristic X-ray production
theory: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference gain kinetic energy. When they strike a target, deceleration can emit a continuous bremsstrahlung spectrum. The maximum photon energy cannot exceed one incoming electron's available kinetic energy; this sets a minimum wavelength. Much of the input energy is transferred as heat rather than X-rays.

Characteristic X-rays arise when inner electron-shell vacancies are filled by electrons from higher energy states. Their photon energies are discrete and depend on the target's atomic energy structure. Raising tube voltage changes the continuous spectrum's energy limit and may enable characteristic emission, but does not continuously shift a fixed target's characteristic line energies.

Imaging and material-analysis applications depend on penetration and interactions with matter. Contrast, detector response and exposure are part of interpreting an image. Keep characteristic lines, the continuous background and the wavelength cutoff distinct when reading a spectrum.

model.q: An X-ray tube accelerates electrons through 40.0 kV. Find maximum photon energy and minimum wavelength using hc = 1240 eV nm.
steps: Maximum electron kinetic energy is eV = 40000 eV.
The maximum possible single-photon energy is 40.0 keV.

guided.q: The tube voltage rises to 80.0 kV. Predict the new minimum wavelength.
steps: λmin is inversely proportional to that energy.
The minimum wavelength halves to 0.0155 nm.

exam.q: Distinguish the continuous X-ray spectrum from characteristic X-ray lines, including the origin of each.
points: The continuous spectrum comes from varying energy transfers during electron deceleration.
Characteristic lines come from discrete atomic electron transitions after inner-shell vacancies form.
Their line energies depend on the target's energy levels rather than simply matching every possible tube voltage.

claim: All X-rays from a tube have the same energy equal to the full electron accelerating energy.

title: Stimulated emission and the laser
theory: Absorption raises an atom to an allowed higher state. Spontaneous emission releases a photon without a triggering incident photon. Stimulated emission occurs when an appropriate photon induces a matching transition, producing another photon with the same frequency, direction and phase in the ideal description. These mechanisms must be distinguished to explain amplification.

A laser requires an energy pump and a population inversion between the relevant states. A resonant optical cavity selects and reinforces suitable light, with a partially transmitting mirror allowing output. The pump provides the energy; the trigger photon does not independently power an unlimited chain of emissions.

Laser light can have narrow spectral width and high coherence, but these features do not imply that every laser has identical wavelength or power. Application answers should connect the desired beam property to the task, such as precise alignment, reading information or concentrating energy.

model.q: A laser transition has energy difference 1.96 eV. Find wavelength using hc = 1240 eV nm and identify the energy source.
steps: The emitted photon energy equals the level difference.
The pumping system replenishes the excited-state energy used in emission.

guided.q: A transition's energy difference doubles. Predict what happens to emitted photon frequency and wavelength.
steps: E = hf makes frequency proportional to transition energy.

exam.q: Explain how stimulated emission and population inversion enable optical amplification without creating energy.
points: An incident matching photon triggers an excited-state transition producing a matching photon.
Population inversion makes stimulated emission exceed absorption for the relevant transition.
A pump supplies and replenishes the stored excitation energy.

claim: A laser amplifies light without requiring an external energy input.

title: Photovoltaic cells and photon-to-electrical energy transfer
theory: A photovoltaic device absorbs suitable photons to create mobile charge carriers in a semiconductor. An internal junction field separates carriers, allowing electrical energy to be delivered to an external circuit. The energy originates in incident radiation. A photon below the relevant absorption threshold generally cannot create the needed carrier excitation in the simple one-photon model.

Increasing suitable illumination can increase generated current, but output also depends on voltage, temperature, device properties and load. Not all incident energy becomes useful electrical output: reflection, incomplete absorption and thermalisation contribute to losses. Use output power VI and compare it with radiant power incident on the active area.

The simplified threshold is linked to the semiconductor band gap, not a metal photoelectric work function. Both involve quantum energy conditions, but the mechanisms and device structures differ. Treat a cell as an energy converter rather than a store that emits previously accumulated sunlight indefinitely.

model.q: A cell of area 0.0200 m² receives irradiance 800 W m⁻² and delivers 0.500 V at 4.00 A. Find efficiency.
steps: Incident power is irradiance × area = 800 × 0.0200 = 16.0 W.
Useful electrical power is VI = 0.500 × 4.00 = 2.00 W.

guided.q: Under the same input, output current falls to 3.00 A while voltage stays 0.500 V. Find the efficiency.

exam.q: Explain why photons below a semiconductor's relevant excitation threshold cannot be assumed to produce normal photocurrent merely by increasing their number.
points: Each photon supplies a discrete energy hf.
A single suitable carrier excitation requires sufficient energy to meet the relevant threshold.
Increasing photon number raises intensity but not each photon's energy in this one-photon model.

claim: Increasing the number of below-threshold photons necessarily increases each photon's energy.

title: LED photon energy, colour and circuit design
theory: An LED emits light when carriers recombine across semiconductor energy states. The photon energy is related to the material's relevant energy separation, so different semiconductor compositions can give different colours. The energy comes from the electrical supply. An LED needs appropriate current limitation and correct bias; its colour is not selected simply by applying any desired supply voltage.

Use E = hf = hc/λ to connect colour with photon energy. A simple energy-gap estimate gives the emitted wavelength, but a real LED has a spectral width and additional electrical losses. Distinguish photon energy, junction voltage and the total supply voltage shared with other components.

A series resistor limits current by taking the voltage remaining after the diode's forward drop. Efficiency compares optical output with electrical input and is not generally 100%. This lesson connects Year 11 circuit modelling with Year 12 discrete energy transitions.

model.q: An idealised LED emits photons of energy 2.00 eV. Estimate wavelength using hc = 1240 eV nm, then find a series resistor for a 5.00 V supply, 2.00 V forward drop and 0.0200 A.
steps: The current-limiting resistance is 150 Ω in the stated operating model.

guided.q: An LED's photon energy is 3.10 eV. Find its approximate wavelength and compare its colour's photon energy with the 2.00 eV model.
steps: The wavelength is shorter than 620 nm.
Its emitted photons have higher energy and higher frequency.

exam.q: Explain why using a higher supply voltage does not simply set any desired LED colour, and identify the function of its series resistor.
points: Photon energy is linked to the semiconductor's relevant energy-state separation.
Changing supply voltage mainly changes the operating current and voltage distribution, not an arbitrary selectable energy gap.
A correctly chosen series resistor limits current by taking the remaining supply voltage.

claim: An LED's colour can always be chosen just by turning its supply voltage up or down.
